input: This case examines the pricing of a SaaS tier and considers whether the tier, at its current price, is selling at a level that comfortably covers its costs. The tier is offered at a price of $361 per unit, while the variable cost of serving each unit amounts to $222 per unit. On top of these variable costs, the business incurs fixed costs of $336k per year, which must be covered irrespective of the volume that is sold. When these figures are brought together, the break-even volume is found to be 2417 units per year, representing the level of sales at which the total contribution generated by the units sold is exactly sufficient to meet the fixed costs. The current volume, encouragingly, stands at 8162 units per year, which is substantially in excess of the break-even requirement. It would nevertheless be a mistake to read these figures as a complete picture of the tier's robustness. The volume figures relied upon are last year's actuals, and they therefore provide a record of how the tier traded in the past rather than a guarantee of how it will trade in the future. In addition, the effect of the price on volume has not been estimated, so the analysis offers no insight into how sensitive the volume might prove to be if the price were adjusted upwards or downwards in response to changing market conditions. These qualifications do not undermine the arithmetic itself, but they do define the limits within which its conclusions can properly be applied in practice.
target: At the current price, the SaaS tier covers its fixed costs well below its present volume. The price is $361 per unit, the variable cost is $222 per unit, and the fixed costs are $336k per year. The contribution of each unit, the price less the variable cost, divided into the fixed costs gives the break-even volume of 2417 units per year. Current volume is 8162 units per year. The margin between the two volumes is the tier's protection against a fall in sales: volume can decline to the break-even point before the tier stops covering its fixed costs. Both volumes are annual figures, and the comparison between them is an annual comparison. The break-even volume separates two regimes for the tier: above it, each additional unit adds its contribution to profit, while below it each unit sold still contributes, but the total contribution no longer reaches the fixed costs. The fixed costs are stated per year and the volume per year, so the comparison is a yearly one and says nothing about the pattern of sales within the year. The statement holds for the price and costs as given, and it inherits two limits from its inputs. The volume figures are last year's actuals, so both the current volume and the comparison it supports describe the tier's past trading. The effect of the price on volume is not estimated; the break-even arithmetic treats volume as independent of price, and a price change large enough to move volume would move the current figure while the calculation stood still. Within those limits, the tier at its present price and cost base covers its fixed costs at a volume far under its present sales.
